newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania to use monetary whip against inflation.
newsitem.headline: Romania to use monetary whip against inflation.

text.p: Romania's central bank has set its monetary policy sights on reining in soaring inflation as the country seeks around $1 billion in new credits from international lenders to underpin radical reforms.

On Monday, central bank (BNR) governor Mugur Isarescu gave a foretaste of monetary policies which will be coupled with a broader reform package that the new government is negotiating with the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

The eventual target is "to slash inflation to an annualised rate of under 30 percent in the second half of 1997," Isarescu told a news conference. "That means a monthly inflation of around 2.0 percent in the last months of 1997."
Inflation surged to a year-on-year 56.9 percent last year, triple the 20 percent target agreed with the Fund.
IMF and World bank experts have been working with the new centrist government for a month as the latter fine-tunes reforms which it hopes will gain Romania a combined $1 billion in fresh credits.
Both lenders suspended credits to Romania last year over foreign exchange market curbs and overspending by the former leftist government in an election year.
"We hope that the new loan talks will conclude with positive results within one week," government spokesman Eugen Serbanescu said at the weekend.

The government, which is facing mounting pressure from trade unions, has pledged to go ahead with plans to privatise and restructure unwieldy, communist-era state industries and to keep budget spending within reasonable limits.
Isarescu said Romania would see quickening inflation in the next few months, led by expected electricity and food price rises.
"Our monetary policy in the first months of 1997 aims to keep inflation under control as price liberalisation will trigger higher, corrective inflation.
"Prices must be aligned (to world levels). It's a sacrifice that we must accept," he added, declining to give an estimate for inflation in the first half of 1997.
Isarescu said the target for 1997 money supply growth, which would be released next week, depended to a great extent on the level of what he called "corrective inflation".
In a bid to temper inflation, the BNR has already lifted key interest rates in its drive to tighten monetary policies.
But the BNR would also make its policies more flexible, by letting market mechanisms have their say, Isarescu said.

On Monday the BNR announced that it would allow the Lombard rate to float, starting this week, in line with the one-week refinancing rate, which jumped to 90 percent last week from a previous 81 percent.

A strong advocate of export-led economic growth, Isarescu said the goal of economic policies in 1997 would be "to achieve a massive reorientation of resources towards exporters", in a bid to make Romania's economic growth sustainable.
"In 1995 and especially last year Romania's economic growth was import-oriented. Such a growth is not sustainable."
Latest statistics showed Romania's economy expanded by 4.1 percent in 1996, down from 7.1 percent the previous year.
Last year's overvalued leu currency also hit exports, which fell 3.2 percent from 1995. The 1996 trade gap was $1.54 billion, almost unchanged from $1.57 billion in 1995.
The leu has weakened by some 58 percent to 6,450/500 to the dollar since January 1 as the central bank has allowed it to gradually head towards a more "realistic" value.
